PMGT1865 Week 03

PMGT1865 Week 03 — Overlapping Networks, Lag and Lead

Activities and Timing

A precedence network represents activities and the timing constraints between them. Overlapping relationships allow a successor to start before its predecessor finishes when the work logic permits this. They can model phased handovers, coordinated starts and coordinated finishes more accurately than finish-to-start links alone.

An activity box normally records its name, duration, early start, early finish, late start, late finish and total float.

Symbol

Meaning

i, j

Predecessor activity i and successor activity j

dᵢ, dⱼ

Durations of activities i and j

ES, EF

Early start and early finish

LS, LF

Late start and late finish

ESD, EFD

Early start date and early finish date; equivalent timing concepts to ES and EF

L

Signed lag attached to a relationship

wᵢⱼ

Minimum separation between the starts of i and j implied by a relationship

For each activity, EF = ES + d and LF = LS + d. All timing values must use consistent calendars and units.

Lag, Lead and Float

• Lag is a required delay between the events connected by a relationship. A positive L delays the constrained successor event.

• Lead allows the constrained successor event to occur earlier; it can be represented as a negative lag.

• Slack, or total float, is scheduling flexibility: total float = LS − ES = LF − EF. It is calculated from the whole network rather than inserted as a relationship delay.

Four Relationship Types

FS, SS, FF and SF are also written FTS, STS, FTF and STF. A relationship gives a lower bound on the successor's timing, not necessarily its final scheduled time: other constraints may require a later start.

For FF and SF, convert the finish constraint to a start constraint by subtracting the successor's duration. With multiple relationships, use the maximum of all applicable lower bounds and any project-start constraint.

Compound SS and FF Constraints

Both relationships can apply to the same activity pair. The successor must satisfy both:

ESⱼ = max(ESᵢ + Lₛₛ, EFᵢ + L𝒻𝒻 − dⱼ), subject to any other constraints.

Here Lₛₛ is the SS lag and L𝒻𝒻 is the FF lag. One relationship controls the early timing if its lower bound is larger; both control when the bounds are equal.

Forward and Backward Calculation Method

Establish the relationships, durations, signed lags and project start.

Convert every relationship to ESⱼ ≥ ESᵢ + wᵢⱼ using the table above.

In the forward pass, set each ES to the largest applicable lower bound, then calculate EF = ES + d.

Set the project finish to the largest required terminal EF.

In the backward pass, each relationship requires LSᵢ ≤ LSⱼ − wᵢⱼ. Take the minimum applicable upper bound, including any required project-finish constraint.

Calculate LF = LS + d and total float = LS − ES.

In a simple acyclic network with fixed durations, the controlling chain of tight relationships determines the project finish. With overlaps, adding the full durations of all activities on that chain can double-count overlapping time. Relationship offsets and lags must remain in the calculation.

The critical path is A → B → D → F. Its controlling timing is 15 days to A's finish, 3 days to B's finish, 2 days of lag before D, 8 days for D and 10 days for F:

15 + 3 + 2 + 8 + 10 = 38 days.

B's full five-day duration is not added again because its start overlaps A. C and E each have 11 days of total float; this is shared flexibility on their branch rather than 22 independent days.
